clue.text: Getting on train for college?

parts.note: boarding a bus or train is getting on it
to train someone is to school them

explanation.surface: A student wonders whether catching a train will get them to college.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Getting on train' reads as climbing aboard a railway carriage; split it, and each part is a synonym. The question mark flags that a college is only loosely this kind of establishment.
explanation.definitionFit: A residential educational establishment where pupils live during term, loosely called a college here.

clue.text: Vegetable one bites into over and over

indicators.note: biting into something puts teeth inside it, so the single letter goes in between

parts.note: over, as in a talk over or on a topic
I is the Roman numeral for one
the second over, again meaning on

explanation.surface: A vegetable is something one bites into again and again.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Over and over' means repeatedly in the surface, but it supplies ON twice, with I between.
explanation.definitionFit: An onion is a bulb vegetable used in cooking around the world.

clue.text: Country tune on the rise across American South

indicators.note: lying across something spans it from side to side, so the tune is placed around the rest
in a down clue, rising means reading from the bottom up, so the word goes backwards

parts.note: an air is a tune
US is short for American
S is the abbreviation for south

explanation.surface: A country song is climbing the charts across the American South.
explanation.walkthrough: AIR flips to RIA, which goes around USS.
explanation.definitionFit: Russia is the largest nation on Earth by area, spanning Europe and Asia.

clue.text: Repacked in dry ice, an explosive device

indicators.note: repacking puts the contents back in a different order, so the letters get rearranged

parts.note: the letters of these words

explanation.surface: A bomb has been concealed in a box of dry ice.
explanation.definitionFit: A firebomb designed to start fires is a type of bomb, so the noun names an explosive device.

clue.text: Opening game — love lost for United?

indicators.note: one thing being lost in exchange for another means a letter swaps out

parts.note: golf is a game
love is zero, O, in tennis scoring
U is the abbreviation for United, as in football club names

explanation.surface: An opening match ends with the side losing their love for Manchester United.
explanation.walkthrough: In GOLF, the O is replaced by U.
explanation.definitionFit: A gulf is a wide gap or chasm, so it is a kind of opening in the land or sea.

clue.text: One counts the cost of America's hierarchy

indicators.note: 'of' means drawn from, so the letters come from within the words that follow

parts.note: spans the end of the first word and the start of the second

explanation.surface: Someone works out what America's ruling order costs.
explanation.definitionFit: A person at a till or bank counter tallies payments, literally counting money and costs.

clue.text: Rambling roses old hosts cut, trimming the ends, wanting bouquet?

indicators.note: a host takes guests in, so one piece holds the other inside
rambling means wandering about aimlessly, so the letters stray from their order

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written

indicators.note: trimming the ends removes the first and last letters, leaving the middle

parts.note: the middle letter of this word

explanation.surface: Climbing roses that have been cut back lose their scent.
explanation.walkthrough: OLD takes in U to make OULD; that and ROSES are rearranged. 'Bouquet' is not flowers but a smell, as with wine.
explanation.definitionFit: Lacking any smell is lacking a bouquet, the word used for the aroma of wine.

clue.text: Right to tuck into beer, compared to being extravagant?

indicators.note: tucking into something places it inside, so the letter goes in among the others

parts.note: lager is a type of beer
R is the abbreviation for right
than is the comparison word
being, existence, is life

explanation.surface: Someone tucks into beer and gets compared to a show-off.
explanation.definitionFit: Something flamboyant or exaggerated is more vivid than ordinary existence, an idiom for extravagance.

clue.text: Often wet clothes dangle about one's masculine chest, beginning to shrink

indicators.note: about means around, so the swaying word wraps around the next pieces

parts.note: to dangle is to hang and swing
one's, read as 'one is', becomes I'M
M is the abbreviation for masculine
a trunk is a large storage chest

indicators.note: the beginning of a word is its first letter, which alone is kept

parts.note: the first letter of this word

explanation.surface: Wet clothing hangs around a man's chest and starts to shrink.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Chest' looks like the body part but is a storage box; 'one's' is read as 'one is', contracted.
explanation.definitionFit: Shorts worn by men for bathing are garments that usually end up soaked, so they are often wet clothes.

clue.text: Curious western howdy-do — no university in Oklahoma!?

parts.note: W is the abbreviation for west or western
a casual greeting, like howdy

indicators.note: 'no university' asks for the university's letter to be taken away from the show's description

parts.note: Oklahoma! is the Rodgers and Hammerstein stage show
U is the standard abbreviation for university

explanation.surface: Someone finds a cowboy greeting odd in a state without a university.
explanation.walkthrough: The exclamation mark belongs to the title Oklahoma!, so the state is really the musical. Remove U from MUSICAL to get MSICAL.
explanation.definitionFit: Curious in the sense of odd or quaint, playfully strange, matches a fanciful or capricious manner.

clue.text: Wash, getting grumpy with piercing cold

indicators.note: something piercing goes right into another thing, so one piece sits inside the other

parts.note: a sour person is bad-tempered
C is the abbreviation for cold on a tap

explanation.surface: Someone having a wash in freezing water turns bad-tempered.
explanation.definitionFit: To scrub something clean vigorously is a forceful kind of washing, so the verbs are synonyms.

clue.text: Fellow joining offspring to fence in island home?

parts.note: a fellow is a man

indicators.note: fencing in an area puts a boundary all round it, so one piece is enclosed

parts.note: a son is a child, one's offspring
I is the abbreviation for island on maps

explanation.surface: A man and his son build a fence around their island property.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark shows a grand house is just one sort of home.
explanation.definitionFit: A large stately house is a particularly grand example of a dwelling, hence the question mark.

clue.text: Savage foiled — rocked after making regular sacrifices

indicators.note: sacrificing at regular intervals means every other letter is given up and the rest are kept

parts.note: the first, third, fifth letters and so on of these two words

explanation.surface: A savage plot was thwarted and shaken after many people had given things up.
explanation.definitionFit: Savage and ferocious both describe violent, wild aggression, so the adjectives are synonyms.

clue.text: Coffees he'd tossed down

indicators.note: tossed things are thrown about and land in disorder, so the letters are rearranged

parts.note: the letters of these words

explanation.surface: A man knocked back his coffees in one go.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Down' seems to mean drunk quickly, but it is the definition meaning sad; this British phrase means fed up.
explanation.definitionFit: Being fed up or disgruntled, in British slang, is feeling low or dejected.

clue.text: Woman like Sinéad O'Connor, slightly short

indicators.note: being just a little short means falling one letter below full length, so the last one goes

parts.note: the singer Sinéad O'Connor came from Ireland

explanation.surface: A woman is compared to the singer Sinéad O'Connor and found to be a little small.
explanation.walkthrough: IRISH loses its final H to leave the girl's name IRIS.
explanation.definitionFit: Iris is a female first name, so a woman could be called this; crosswords often clue names this way.

clue.text: Hoping one could perhaps pot red, Ron is missing all ends up

indicators.note: in a down clue, going up means reading from the bottom, so the letters run backwards
missing the ends means the outermost letters of the run are dropped, leaving letters hidden inside

parts.note: the letters of these words with the outer P and S dropped

explanation.surface: A snooker player hopes he might pot the red, but Ron keeps missing.
explanation.walkthrough: In snooker the red is one of the balls to be potted; the surface is about a missed shot, not missing letters.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase introduces a purpose, as in acting so that one might achieve something, which is hoping one could.

clue.text: Leading minister stoned, performing strip taking ecstasy

parts.note: someone stoned on drugs is high

indicators.note: performing suggests acting out something, so the letters are put through new moves

parts.note: taken as written
E is slang for the drug ecstasy

explanation.surface: A senior churchman is caught on drugs, doing a striptease while on ecstasy.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Strip' looks like undressing, but it is just letters to be rearranged along with the drug's letter.
explanation.definitionFit: The chief priest, as in Judaism, is the top cleric, so a leading minister of religion.

clue.text: Polish sign language interpretation guides

parts.note: to polish something gives it a gloss
Aries is a sign of the zodiac

explanation.surface: Someone is looking for guides to interpreting Polish sign language.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Polish' looks like the nationality but is the verb meaning shine; 'sign' looks attached to 'language' but is a star sign.
explanation.definitionFit: Lists of difficult terms with explanations help readers interpret words, so they serve as guides to meaning.

clue.text: Slumped around last month in part of cruise ship?

indicators.note: around means encircling, so the month is placed inside the other word

parts.note: slumped down is sunk
December is the last month of the year

explanation.surface: Someone slumped in a deckchair aboard a cruise liner last month.
explanation.definitionFit: An open upper level on a liner where passengers sunbathe is one area of the vessel.

clue.text: Rescue crew's round is over wide area

indicators.note: turned over means flipped, so the little word is read backwards
going round something encloses it, so the crew's letters wrap the other piece

parts.note: the AA, the Automobile Association, is the British breakdown rescue service
taken as written

explanation.surface: A rescue team's patrol takes in a very large region.
explanation.walkthrough: The AA (Automobile Association) is a British motoring organisation that sends out roadside breakdown crews.
explanation.definitionFit: The largest continent is the biggest expanse of land on Earth, cheekily called a wide area.

clue.text: Have a ball taking in a show

indicators.note: taking something in absorbs it, so the article goes inside the other word

parts.note: to have a ball is to enjoy oneself, to revel
taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone enjoys themselves enormously while seeing a show.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Show' looks like a theatre production but it is the verb meaning disclose.
explanation.definitionFit: To show is to disclose or uncover something hidden, so the two verbs are synonyms.

clue.text: Unlikable beast in hospital dept, going after staff

indicators.note: following something means coming later, so the department's letters are placed second

parts.note: a staff or stick is a rod
ENT is the ear, nose and throat department of a hospital

explanation.surface: A nasty animal loose in a hospital department chases the staff.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Staff' looks like hospital employees, but it is a stick.
explanation.definitionFit: Rats and mice are gnawing mammals that many people find unpleasant, so an unlikable beast fits.

clue.text: Timeless English, like mother but not ma

parts.note: E is the abbreviation for English

indicators.note: 'but not' excludes what follows, so those letters are removed from the word before

parts.note: maternal means motherly
taken as written

explanation.surface: Classic English style is compared to a mother, though not to mum herself.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Ma' is removed from the front of the motherly word, not from anywhere else.
explanation.definitionFit: Something everlasting has no beginning or end and so stands outside time altogether.

clue.text: Sweet packed with energy for relative

indicators.note: packed with means filled with, so the extra letter goes inside

parts.note: sweet, pleasant, is nice
E is the symbol for energy in physics

explanation.surface: An energy-packed confectionery is bought for a family member.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Sweet' looks like a confection but is the adjective meaning pleasant.
explanation.definitionFit: A brother's or sister's daughter is a family member, so a relative.

clue.text: Diagram of flat with no one in

indicators.note: having nobody inside means the single letter standing for one is taken out

parts.note: a plain is flat land
I is the Roman numeral for one

explanation.surface: An architect's drawing of an apartment that nobody lives in.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Flat' looks like an apartment but is level land; PLAIN loses its I.
explanation.definitionFit: A scale drawing showing the layout of a building is a kind of technical diagram.

clue.text: Bottle Romeo's filling still overturned

indicators.note: turned upside down in a down-or-across sense means the word runs backwards
a filling goes inside something, so Romeo's letter sits within the other word

parts.note: still, as in 'still better', can be even
Romeo is R in the NATO phonetic alphabet

explanation.surface: Romeo fills a still that has been knocked over.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bottle' is not a container but British slang for courage.
explanation.definitionFit: In British slang, bottle is courage, and having the nerve to do something means the same.

clue.text: Not bound to release documents being held?

parts.note: to loose something is to set it free
a leaf is a single sheet of paper, such as one held in a ring binder

explanation.surface: Someone is not obliged to hand over papers that are being kept.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Not bound' seems to mean not obliged; it actually describes pages not stitched into a book.
explanation.definitionFit: Sheets kept in a ring binder rather than sewn or glued into a spine are unbound pages.

clue.text: Female member that's gifted?

parts.note: surface reading: a talented woman belonging to some club or society
setter's reading: a woman's leg, which fills the hosiery she wears; 'gifted' points to the small Christmas present of the same name

explanation.walkthrough: The surface invites a talented club member. Read literally, the item that fills a woman's hosiery is her leg, and the phrase is also the small gift found in a Christmas sock.
explanation.definitionFit: A small present put into a Christmas sock is what this phrase means, and a leg literally fills hosiery.
